answer: Use the Receiving Secure Channel command: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The state attribute is the one that answers 'in use': it is the state of the secure channel as returned by the MKA stack, with values in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) and not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). The AID is built from name, a string of length 0..64, plus index, the Receiving Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. sc-rx is show-only and is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

sc-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel object and it is show-only; there is no add, set or delete form. The syntax is show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number], available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. name is a string of length 0..64 and index is the Transmitting Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. state is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack: in-use means Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, not-in-use means none are. It also reports association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number.

A secure-application uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Assign it with set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>; id is a string 0..20, active-certificate-id a string 0..128, and multiple certificates may be listed comma-separated, e.g. set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. show secure-application-<id> reports type (server or client), active-certificate-id, in-use (leafref to active-certificate-id), status (enabled or disabled) and verify-client-cert. To require a client certificate set verify-client-cert required, meaning the client certificate is required and validated, as TLS Mutual Authentication needs; the default is disabled, where no client certificate is requested. Changes take effect only for new TLS connections. show secure-applications lists all of them.

Only if you tell it to. The secure-entity attribute re-key-fail-policy indicates the NE's action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful; the values are kill-traffic and continue-traffic, and the default is continue-traffic, so by default traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset controls how long the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; range 0..86400 seconds, default 0. The related re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end IKE peer, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800. All three are settable on add or set, e.g. add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is a show-only object: show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group], in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Every algorithm attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: number is 1, encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length is key-length-256, integrity-algorithm is none, and dh-group is ecp-521. The integrity-algorithm and dh-group values are the ones advertised to the far-end secure entity peer. So the layer 1 wavelength encryption proposal is fixed at AES-GCM-16 with a 256-bit key and ECP-521, and can only be displayed.

Through the security-policy-database object, whose key is the IKE peer and whose payload is the secure entity. The AID is security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>: ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance and ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA). The associated-secure-entity attribute is the list of all SPD entries associated with that far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). Use add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Example on 1830 GX G40: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1.

Yes, with a CRL Distribution Point: each manually configured CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Use add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>], plus set, delete and show cdps. url is the HTTP URL of the CRL, format http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>, e.g. http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true/false, default false) turns on automatic download and periodic refresh, and enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download; when disabled no refresh occurs but existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval is either the enum use-next-update, taking the next refresh time from the CRL's next-update field, or a duration '[xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs]', e.g. 2w or 5d 12h. show cdp-<name> reports next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result. Requires System Administrator privilege.

Use cert-gen, in Operational mode: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128. Validity is set by days, the number of days the certificate is valid for, and it defaults to 365. org-name is a string 1..64, common-name is the IP or host name identifying the server (1..64), and subject is the full certificate subject name (1..1024); when generating a self-signed certificate you must specify either subject or common-name. auto-install defaults to true and auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application that has no active certificate. -f forces the command without confirmation. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

Through cert-to-name, a prioritized set of rules mapping an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity; each rule either extracts a username from a certificate field or maps it directly. Syntax: add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>], plus set, show and delete. map-type is extract or map. field applies only when map-type is extract: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn, san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map, naming the local or remote user identity. criteria defines the conditions that invoke the rule. priority ranges 1 to 255. issuer (value any) filters certificates from a specific issuer. enabled defaults to True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Delete with clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>, in Operational mode. type is trusted, local or peer, and id is the certificate ID, a string of length 0..128 that must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; press <tab> to list the certificate-ids that can be cleared, and -f skips the confirmation prompt. Examples: clear certificate local certX, or clear certificate type=trusted id=certY. type also accepts bulk purge options instead of a single type: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. To list what is installed, use show certificates, which displays all managed local/trusted/peer X509v3 certificates on the system that were imported by download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles. show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations.

Use the clear form of crl with a clear-target: clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>, in Operational mode. clear-target values are single-crl (default; removes only the CRL named in <crl-name>, which is then mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), purge-invalid-crls (purge all invalid CRLs), purge-cached-crls (purge all CRLs automatically cached from a configured CDP or certificate CDP extension) and purge-all-crls. To drop only stale entries run clear crl purge-invalid-crls, which leaves valid CRLs in place. Use <tab> on crl-name to list clearable CRLs, -f to force without confirmation. Check first with show crls or show crl-<name>, which report status (valid, expired, future), type (cached or manually), next-update and associated-cdp. Example: clear crl single-crl myCA-1.

csr-gen creates a local-certificate in the 'pending-import' state and outputs a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is used with an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is then downloaded into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. The command runs in Operational mode: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>]. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256 (also rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096, eccp128, eccp384, eccp521). signature-hash-algorithm defaults to sha256 for rsa2048/rsa3072/eccp256, sha384 for eccp384, sha512 for rsa4096/eccp521. metadata-template defaults to generic. Default key-usage is digitalSignature,keyAgreement; default extended-key-usage serverAuth,clientAuth. Minimal call: csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia'.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>, in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. display-type accepts all-certificate-hierarchy, certificate-details and certificate-hierarchy, defaulting to all-certificate-hierarchy, so the hierarchy is what you get if you specify nothing; use certificate-details for the certificate's own fields only. certificate names the certificate or CSR, e.g. display-cert trusted-certificate-ca_root; typing display-cert alone tab-completes entries such as local-certificate-pace_client and trusted-certificate-ca_root. The details output is the full X.509 dump: version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity Not Before/Not After, subject, public key info and X509v3 extensions. local-certificate and peer-certificate also expose a trust-chain attribute.

Use the est command. Enrollment over Secure Transport automates certificate requests, renewals and management over HTTPS, replacing the manual CSR process; the device has an EST client that talks to a dedicated EST server. Syntax: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command is cacerts, enroll or re-enroll. est-ca defaults to 1. key-algorithm accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096. signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256. metadata-template defaults to generic. Use http-user and http-password when no valid mTLS certificate exists: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via est-ca: set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>], with a matching show. auto-re-enrollment specifies when re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by that EST CA: a number of days before expiration from 1 to 365, or a percentage of the 'not after date' minus 'not before date' interval rounded up, 10% to 90% in 10% increments, or disabled. The default is Disabled. If auto re-enrollment fails, the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until successful or the certificate becomes invalid. The CA is pinned by explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, and root-fingerprint, a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash verifying the Root CA identity for a secure initial connection. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40.

The EST server port is server-port and it defaults to 443. Define servers with add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], with set, delete and show forms in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Yes, you can define more than one: priority defines the server's precedence and takes a value in the range 1 to 10. If priority is omitted it defaults to the current lowest precedence, that is the highest existing number, plus one; if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. server-address is the IP address of the EST server, enabled is True or False with default True, and path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base url, a string of length 0..64. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format into the NE, in Operational mode: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]. The PEM string is supplied inline. certificate-name is the name the certificate will be known by; if omitted, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, e.g. trusted-certificate-Nokia-1, trusted-certificate-Nokia-2. passphrase decodes encrypted input and applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. -i imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM string bundle, and for single-certificate files imports intermediates specified through the AIA extension; root certificates must be installed individually. -h shows help. Example: import-certificate peer-certificate certificate-name=peer-cert1 <string in PEM format>.

Check the is-key-in-use attribute on the Image Signing Key: show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], or show ISKs for the list. is-key-in-use indicates if the key is in use in this FRU; true/false, default false. is-key-verified indicates if the key is verified in this FRU; true/false, default false. being-deleted is set to true once the system gets an ISK delete command, meaning deletion is in progress. Remove one with clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>, key-name being a string 0..64 and -f forcing without confirmation. Access is Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode only for show. Example: show ISK-1-5-0-ISK_E1.

Use the KRK commands, which show the list of Image Root Keys (KRKs) and KRK information: show KRKs for the full list, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] for one key, for example show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The attributes are name, the unique representation of the object; CPU, the identifier for member CPUs on cards, starting at 0 (uint8); key-name, a string of length 0..64; key-serial-number, a string; issuer-name, the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a string of length 0..20; key-length in bits (uint16); and key-payload, the key payload in hex format, a string of length 0..1100. KRK is show-only. The related ISK object reports KRK-name, the name of the KRK that signed that Image Signing Key.

show key-replacement-package displays the key replacement package (KRP) attributes, in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode; it is show-only. Full form: show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. install-status indicates whether this KRP has been installed in the system: not-installed, installing, installed, failed. KRP-version is the package version. issuer-name is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), string 0..20. KRK-name is the name of the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK. signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none; signature-payload is a hex string 0..1024.

Yes, with the revocation-mode attribute of local-certificate: set local-certificate-<id> revocation-mode force-revoked. revocation-mode controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and takes auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, default auto; force-unrevoked is the opposite override. The same set also accepts alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and label (string 0..256). id is a string 1..128. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. show local-certificate-<id> reports revocation-mode plus status (valid, revoked, expired, untrusted, future, pending-import) and used-by, the list of secure-applications, ikev2-peers and similar presently using the certificate. peer-certificate has the identical revocation-mode attribute, values and default.

Add one with add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>], in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode; priority is mandatory on add. Order is set by priority, a uint8 in the range 1..10, which sorts the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, so priority 1 is tried first. url is the HTTP URL of the responder, format http://<host>[:<port>], host being an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and port optional, otherwise the default HTTP port 80 is used; length 0..1024. enabled controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status; true/false, default false, so a new responder must be enabled explicitly. name is a string 0..64. Reorder later with set ocsp-server-<name> priority <value>. show ocsp-server-<name> reports url, enabled, priority and last-query. Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted 'remote peer' certificate for the L1 encryption secure application. white-listed is read-only in show peer-certificate[-id]: if true, the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain. Values true/false, default false. The only settable attributes are alarm-report-control (inhibited or allowed, default allowed), label (string 0..256) and revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked, default auto). show also returns version (v3), serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length, public-key-type, certificate-bytes, subject-alternative-names, key-usage and extended-key-usage. status values are revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future, valid and unsupported.

The ssh object controls secure shell access; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Use set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>] and show ssh, in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. port is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell; range 1..65535, default 8022. enabled enables direct access to shell via ssh; true or false, default false, so it is off by default and must be turned on explicitly. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login, a string 0..1440 with no default. post-login-message is displayed after login, also 0..1440, and has a default banner warning that the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and may be monitored.

Add an ssh-authorized-key for that user; each entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Syntax: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>], with set ... [label <value>], show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label] and delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. user-name owns the key and can be a local or remote user, string 0..32; key-id is a unique identifier for the entry, 1..64. public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component in PEM format, <key type><SPACE>base64 encoded OpenSSH public key<SPACE><comment>, up to 2048 characters. public-key-algorithm is show-only: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096.
